Varve counter — manual

A complete guide from an empty folder to a varve chronology with uncertainties, final depths and varve thicknesses. It covers how to work together with coauthors and why the tool works the way it does. The technical design is in DESIGN.md; a short overview is in README.md.

1. What the tool does

You count varve boundaries on scanned thin sections. Several people count the same sections independently. The tool then:

  • matches their boundaries and decides which ones are varves, following Method C of Żarczyński, Tylmann & Goslar (2018, Quaternary Geochronology 47: 107–119);
  • gives each varve a core depth in the composite profile, with cracks left out;
  • measures varve thickness across the width of the section.
 Step A  Project       people, sections (one image per thin section)
 Step B  Setup         DPI, counting path, core depths            → project file
 Step C  1 Count       each counter, blind                        → one counts file per person
 Step D  2 Decide      match counts, majority rule, review        → chronology file
 Step E  3 Final (1)   cracks on the path → final varve depths    → Module 3 file, varves.csv
 Step F  3 Final (2)   horizons → varve thickness                 → thickness.csv

Typical roles:

Role Does Writes
Project lead (one person) Steps A, B, D, E, F project file, chronology, Module 3 file
Counter (usually three people, the lead can be one of them) Step C own counts file

2. Before you start

Software. Only a web browser. The whole tool is one file, index.html; double-click it and it opens. Nothing is installed and nothing is uploaded: images and data stay on your computer, and the tool works offline.

  • Chrome or Edge are recommended. They can save a file back to where it came from (“save in place”). Firefox and Safari work too, but every save becomes a download that you move into the project folder yourself.

Images. One scan per thin section.

  • Formats: TIFF (uncompressed, LZW, Deflate or PackBits; 8 or 16 bit; strips or tiles), BMP, PNG, JPEG.
  • Not supported: JPEG-compressed TIFF, BigTIFF, floating-point TIFF. Re-save such files as uncompressed or LZW TIFF before you start (see 12.4 — images must not change later).
  • Size: a 10 cm thin section at 2400 DPI (about 9,500 × 1,900 px) is easy. Very large stitched scans (over about 20,000 px on a side) may exceed browser limits.
  • Scan resolution (DPI) is read from the file. Write it down from the scanner settings anyway: scanners often store a wrong or default value.

What you need to know about the core. For each thin section, the core depth (in the composite profile) where your counting line starts and ends. Section 5.3 explains how to choose these.

Suggested folder. Put everything of one profile in one folder (details in 12.1):

ZAB-12/
  index.html                     ← the tool (a copy, so everyone uses the same version)
  manual.html                    ← this manual (opened by the tool's “Manual” link)
  images/                        ← the thin-section scans, never edited
  ZAB-12.project.json
  counts/                        ← one file per counter
  ZAB-12.chronology.json
  ZAB-12.thickness.json
  exports/                       ← CSV and PNG exports

3. Key ideas in five minutes

  • Project. One composite sediment profile, e.g. ZAB-12. Its name is part of every file name and is how files recognise each other.
  • Section. One thin section = one image. Sections are ordered from top to bottom.
  • Path. The counting line drawn on a section. It can be made of several segments (to step around a disturbance); they are joined into one length.
  • s. Position along the path, from its start.
  • Depth anchors. The core depth of the path start (top) and end (base). Every point on the path gets a core depth by linear interpolation between them; this corrects shrinkage of the thin section and small correlation errors.
  • Boundary. One click = one varve boundary. A boundary is the base of the varve above it, i.e. the point where that varve year begins (for example, the start of the spring calcite lamina on top of the previous winter layer).
  • Counting goes from the top down. Varve 1 is the youngest varve, at the top of the record (the year of coring, possibly incomplete). The partial varve below the last boundary at the base of the record is not counted.
  • Varve numbers only. The tool never assigns calendar years. Anchoring to the coring year, a tephra or radiocarbon is done later (e.g. in R). Floating chronologies need no special treatment.
  • People have short ids (P1, MZ, …) that appear in all files and exports.

4. Step A — Create the project

  1. Open index.html.
  2. Project → New, enter the profile name (e.g. ZAB-12).
    • Choose it carefully: counts and chronology files check that they belong to this exact name. Renaming later separates the project from files made with the old name.
  3. People → + Add person for everyone who will count or work on the project. Give short, stable ids; names are optional.
    • Ids end up in file names and exports. Use letters, digits, - or _.
  4. I am (top of the panel): choose yourself. The browser remembers this per project.
  5. + Add sections…: choose all thin-section images at once.
    • Each image becomes a section named after the file (you can rename it in Setup).
    • Order them top to bottom with ↑ ↓.
    • The project stores each image's name and its SHA-256 hash (a fingerprint of the file's content), not the image itself.
  6. Save → ZAB-12.project.json.

Why images are not stored in the project: a project file of a few kB is easy to send and version; scans are hundreds of MB. The hash guarantees that everybody works on exactly the same image, whatever the file is called on their computer.

5. Step B — Set up each section

Done once, by one person, in the Setup tab. Choose the section at the top of the tab.

5.1 Resolution (DPI)

  • DPI shows the value read from the image and its source (image header).
  • If it is wrong or missing, type the correct value (entered by hand).
  • Or Calibrate from a scale bar…: click both ends of a scale bar visible on the scan, type its length in mm, Apply (scale bar).

Why it matters: DPI converts pixels to millimetres for thicknesses and positions. Core depths come from the depth anchors (5.3), so a slightly wrong DPI does not shift depths, but it does change thicknesses. The stretch factor (5.3) is your check.

5.2 The counting path

  1. Draw segment. Click points along the line on which you want varves to be counted, from top to bottom of the section. Finish with Enter, a double-click or a right-click. Esc cancels.
  2. Choose the line where lamination is clearest and most continuous. It does not have to be straight; add points to follow it.
  3. More segments (to step around a disturbance, a burrow, a bad patch): draw the next segment the same way. It must start on the same lamina where the previous segment ended, only shifted sideways.
    • A pink joint guide runs through the end of the previous segment, across the path, roughly along that lamina. The first click of the new segment snaps onto it. Check that the guide really follows the lamina; hold Shift while clicking to place the start freely.
    • Segments are joined into one length: the first segment covers s = 0 … L1, the second L1 … L1+L2, and so on.
  4. Move / edit mode: drag a point to move it; right-click or Delete removes it. The segment list on the left can delete whole segments.

Why joints must be on the same lamina: the joined path is one continuous axis of depth. If the second segment started on a different lamina, the varves in between would be skipped or counted twice.

Ownership rule: a segment owns its start but not its end. A boundary exactly on a joint is counted once, in the following segment.

5.3 Core depth of the path

Enter Path start (top) and Path end (base) in cm of composite core depth.

  • Usually you determine these from the correlation of the thin section with the core (e.g. marker layers, the position of the thin-section box in the core).
  • The path end of a section must equal the path start of the next one. When you enter a base depth, the next section's empty top depth is filled with the same value. The Project tab shows a green message when depths are continuous, or the gap/overlap that must be fixed.
  • Because thin sections overlap (typically by about 2 cm), choose the joint so that the path of section n ends exactly on the lamina where the path of section n+1 starts. Then no varve is counted twice or skipped.

The panel shows the stretch factor = depth interval ÷ path length in mm. Values near 1 are normal (slightly above 1 when the thin section shrank). Values far from 1 (the tool warns beyond ±15 %) usually mean a wrong DPI or wrong depths.

Why linear interpolation between two anchors: it spreads the difference between the thin section and the core evenly over the section, so errors do not accumulate from one section to the next. Cracks are corrected separately and later (Step E), because they are local.

Save the project when all sections are set up. Freeze the setup before counting (see 12.5): changing a path afterwards is possible, but counters' boundaries then have to be re-attached to the new path.

6. Step C — Count (Module 1)

Each counter, independently.

  1. Open index.html, Project → Open… the project file.
  2. Load images…: select the scans (all at once is fine). They are recognised by their content; file names do not matter.
  3. I am: choose yourself.
  4. Tab 1 Count → New count (first time) or Open… your counts file (ZAB-12.P2.counts.json).
  5. Choose a section and click every varve boundary you see.
    • Clicks snap to the path. You may click beside the path on the same boundary; it is projected onto the path.
    • Drag a mark to move it; right-click or Delete removes it; Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo / redo.
    • A click beyond the path end is refused: that boundary belongs to the next section.
    • Navigation: wheel = zoom, drag = pan, D / A = move along the path deeper / back, F = fit, R = rotate the view, brightness and contrast at the top right.
    • The panel shows the number of boundaries, the selected boundary's core depth and the thickness of the varve above it.
  6. Save often (Ctrl+S). One file holds all your sections.
  7. Optionally Export CSV for your own checks.

Rules for counters

  • Count blind. Do not look at other people's counts until all counting is finished; the tool only ever shows your own marks in this tab.
  • Mark every boundary you see, once. There is no “uncertain” flag on purpose: Method C estimates uncertainty from disagreement between counters. If you are unsure, decide for yourself; that is exactly the information the method needs.
  • Use the same criterion for a boundary throughout (agreed beforehand, e.g. from the microfacies description).

Why blind: if counters see each other's marks, their counts are no longer independent and agreement between them no longer measures uncertainty.

7. Step D — Decide the varves (Module 2, Method C)

Done by the project lead, after all counts are finished (this tab shows everyone's marks).

7.1 Load and match

  1. Open the project and images. Tab 2 Decide.
  2. Load counts files…: select all counters' files at once. Each counter gets a colour.
  3. Check the settings (defaults are usually fine):
    • Tolerance × local varve thickness (0.5): two marks of different counters can be the same boundary only if they are closer than this fraction of the local varve thickness.
    • Window (10): how many neighbouring boundaries the local thickness is computed from (running median of the spacing).
  4. Match automatically.

Why a tolerance relative to varve thickness: varve thickness changes along the profile (e.g. from about 2 mm to over 6 mm in Lake Żabińskie). A fixed distance would be too strict for thick varves and too loose for thin ones. At 0.5, a mark is never matched to a boundary that is closer to its neighbour.

Why the order is preserved: boundaries are matched by an alignment that never lets two matched groups cross; this mirrors how a person would pair counts side by side.

7.2 The decision rule

For each matched group, n of N counters marked it (N = counters who counted that section; the panel warns when someone did not):

Agreement Decision Uncertainty
all counters varve —
majority (more than half) varve negative +1
minority (half or fewer) not a varve positive +1

Positive and negative uncertainties are summed separately from the top of the record down, giving ranges such as 2028 +34/−53. With three counters the majority is 2; with four, 3; a 2–2 tie is not a majority.

Why this rule: it is Method C of the paper. Every boundary is judged on its own, there is no master count, no half-years and no arbitrary decision. Asymmetric uncertainty is a real result: it tells you whether the chronology is more likely too short or too long.

7.3 Review

On the image every counter has a track (coloured dots) and matched marks are linked: green = all agree, yellow = majority, red ring = rejected. Varve numbers are on one side; a ? marks groups that need review.

A group is flagged when not all counters agree, when its marks are far apart (over 80 % of the tolerance), or when it is new (see 7.5).

  • Next ▸ / ◂ Prev (keys . and ,) jump from flag to flag across sections.
  • Click a mark to select its group; the panel shows who marked it, where, and the decision.
  • Detach (X): takes the selected mark out of its group (it was matched wrongly).
  • Shift+click a mark of another group: merges the two groups. Refused when both contain a mark of the same counter, or when the result would put one counter's boundaries out of order.
  • Checked (C): marks the group as reviewed; with only unchecked ticked, Next skips it.
  • Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo / redo.

You correct the matching only. The decision always follows the majority rule and cannot be changed by hand.

Why decisions cannot be overridden: that is what keeps Method C objective. If a reviewer could promote or reject boundaries, the result would again depend on one person.

7.4 Save and export

  • Save → ZAB-12.chronology.json: the matching, every manual edit (with who and when), the settings, and the resolved positions needed by Module 3.
  • Export CSV → ZAB-12.chronology.csv (see 11).

7.5 Re-running and changed counts

  • Re-run matching (e.g. after changing the tolerance) asks whether to keep the groups you edited by hand.
  • If a counter later changes their counts and you open the chronology with the new files, boundaries that no longer exist are removed from their groups and new boundaries are added as single groups flagged new. Review them, save again.
  • A chronology can only be opened together with the counts of every counter it was built from.

8. Step E — Final depths (Module 3, step 1)

  1. Tab 3 Final → Open chronology… (ZAB-12.chronology.json), or Take from 2 Decide when you have just made it in the same session. The counts files are not needed here.
  2. Tool 1 · Cracks on path. Wherever a crack crosses the path, click its upper edge, then its lower edge. A pink band shows it.
    • Drag an edge to adjust it; right-click or Delete removes a crack.
    • Overlapping cracks are refused.
  3. When a section is done, tick All cracks on the path are marked in this section, also when it has no cracks.
  4. Save → ZAB-12.thickness.json (the Module 3 file; it also holds Step F).
  5. Export varves CSV (final depths) and Export cracks CSV.

The section panel shows the stretch factor with and without cracks.

Why cracks are handled only here: all counters count on the same image, so a crack shifts everyone's positions equally and does not affect matching. It does add its width to the path length; leaving it out gives the true core depth of every varve below it.

Why the “complete” tick: it is exported as crack_corrected, so a section with no cracks is distinguishable from a section nobody checked.

9. Step F — Varve thickness (Module 3, step 2)

Thickness is measured across the width of the section, not only on the path.

9.1 Horizons (default)

  1. Tool 2 · Horizons. Select a boundary: click its mark on the path, or ◂ / ▸ Boundary (keys [ ]).
  2. Click a few points along that lamina, on both sides of the path; finish with Enter, a double-click or a right-click. The boundary's mark on the path is added automatically. With Go to the next boundary ticked, the next boundary is selected.
  3. Once both boundaries of a varve have horizons, its thickness appears in the panel:
    • at 3 positions (a setting, 1–10) spread across the width where both horizons exist: the shortest distance from the base horizon to the top horizon;
    • an area mean: the area between the two horizons divided by their shared width.

Why horizons: a line “drawn at an angle” is only a true thickness when it is perpendicular to the lamina, which is a guess on bent laminae. The shortest distance between two traced boundaries is perpendicular to the lamina by definition.

Why one horizon per boundary: each boundary is the base of the varve above and the top of the varve below, so it is traced once and used twice.

9.2 Cracks

  • Crack along a boundary (the common case): before tracing that boundary, tick Crack along this boundary, trace the crack's upper edge (Enter), then its lower edge (Enter). The upper edge is the base of the varve above, the lower edge the top of the varve below; the crack belongs to neither.
  • Crack inside a varve: tool Cracks in varves, trace the upper edge (Enter), then the lower edge (Enter). Its width is subtracted from that varve at each position.

9.3 Quick lines (fallback)

For simple, parallel laminae, or where horizons are not possible: tool Quick lines, click the base and then the top of a varve. The line is assigned to the varve containing its midpoint. To subtract a crack on a line: select the line, Crack on line (K), click the crack's two ends.

The first varve of each section cannot be measured with horizons (its top boundary lies in the previous image). Use a quick line there.

9.4 Export

Export thickness CSV → ZAB-12.thickness.csv; Save the Module 3 file.

Thickness is given in px, in mm (from DPI) and in mm corrected for the stretch factor (consistent with core depths).

10. Exporting images

Export… (top right, or E) in any tab saves the current section with whatever is marked at that moment, including unsaved work. A preview shows the result.

  • Default: the whole section at full resolution, original orientation. Marks and labels are sized in millimetres on the section, so they stay readable when printed; adjust with Mark and label size.
  • Current view only: exactly what is on screen (zoom, rotation, brightness).
  • Layers (path, marks, numbers, labels), brightness/contrast, a scale bar and a caption strip (project, section, module, person, date, depths, counts) can be switched.
  • The PNG stores the DPI, so it keeps its scale in other software.
  • What is drawn follows the tab: Setup = the path; 1 Count = only your own boundaries; 2 Decide = all counters, matching and varve numbers; 3 Final = cracks, final varves, horizons and measurements.

Images are for figures, notes and discussion. The JSON and CSV files remain the record.

11. The output files and how to use them

File Written in One row per Main columns
…P2.counts.csv 1 Count boundary of one counter section, person, seq, s_mm, core_depth_mm
chronology.csv 2 Decide matched group varve_no, included, status, n_agree, n_counters, persons, core_depth_mm, top_mm, bottom_mm, unc_pos_cum, unc_neg_cum
varves.csv 3 Final final varve varve_no, status, top_depth_mm, bottom_depth_mm, bottom_depth_uncorrected_mm, unc_pos_cum, unc_neg_cum, crack_corrected
cracks.csv 3 Final crack on the path s_upper_mm, s_lower_mm, width_mm, core_depth_mm
thickness.csv 3 Final measurement varve_no, method, position_no, thickness_mm, thickness_corr_mm, crack_px

Notes:

  • Depths are in mm of composite core depth; varves.csv depths are crack-corrected.
  • unc_pos_cum / unc_neg_cum are cumulative from the top of the record. Ages, if you need them, are e.g. coring_year − varve_no + 1, with the uncertainty range from these columns.
  • In thickness.csv, method is horizon (one row per position), horizon_area (area mean) or line. Keep methods apart when summarising.
  • Rejected groups in chronology.csv have an empty varve_no; they are kept because they carry the positive uncertainty.

Reading them in R, for example:

library(tidyverse)

varves <- read_csv("ZAB-12.varves.csv")
thickness <- read_csv("ZAB-12.thickness.csv") |>
  filter(method == "horizon") |>
  summarise(thickness_mm = mean(thickness_corr_mm), n = n(), .by = varve_no)

varves |>
  left_join(thickness, by = "varve_no")

The JSON files are plain text and can be read with jsonlite::read_json() when you need the full detail (e.g. the edit log of the matching).

12. Working with coauthors: sharing and portability

12.1 The project package

Everything is ordinary files. A project is portable when these travel together:

File Needed by Written by
index.html and manual.html everyone — (keep one copy of each in the folder)
images everyone — (never change them)
ZAB-12.project.json everyone project lead
counts/ZAB-12.<id>.counts.json project lead (Step D) each counter, own file only
ZAB-12.chronology.json Step E/F project lead
ZAB-12.thickness.json Step E/F project lead (or whoever measures)

Files are found through the open dialogs, so the folder can live anywhere (a USB stick, a network drive, a cloud folder) and be organised as you like. The tool never needs a fixed path.

12.2 Distributing a project to counters

  1. Finish and save Steps A–B. Freeze the project file from now on (12.5).
  2. Send each counter: index.html, the images and ZAB-12.project.json (a zip, a shared folder or a USB stick).
  3. Each counter adds their id in I am, counts (Step C), saves ZAB-12.<id>.counts.json and sends only that file back.
  4. The project lead collects all counts files in counts/ and continues with Step D.

Counters never need each other's files, and should not see them before Step D.

12.3 Shared folders (Dropbox, OneDrive, Nextcloud, Google Drive, network drive)

Working in one shared folder is convenient and safe if everyone writes only their own files:

  • Counters write only counts/ZAB-12.<their id>.counts.json.
  • Only the project lead saves the project, chronology and Module 3 files.
  • Do not open and save the same file on two computers at the same time; the last save wins.
  • With Chrome or Edge, Save writes back into the shared folder. With other browsers, move the downloaded file into the folder, replacing the old one.

12.4 Rules that keep files linked

Do not Why If it happened
Edit, re-save, convert or compress an image after adding it The SHA-256 changes and the tool refuses the image (“content differs”) Use the original file. If the original is lost, add the new image as a new section and redo its setup.
Rename the project Counts and chronology files check the project name Rename it back.
Change a path after counting has started Counts are re-attached to the nearest segment; small shifts are possible Avoid; if necessary, tell everyone and re-check in Step D.
Change person ids after counting Ids are written into the counts files Keep ids stable.
Use different versions of index.html Newer versions read older files, but mixed versions are harder to trace Keep one copy of index.html in the project folder.

Renaming image files or sections, and moving folders, is harmless: images are recognised by content, and counts follow a renamed section by its image hash.

12.5 Freezing a project

There is no lock button; freezing is an agreement: after the project file is sent to counters, only the project lead changes it, and only for things that do not move paths (for example adding a person). Keep a dated copy (e.g. ZAB-12.project.2026-11-24.json) of the version that was sent out.

12.6 Moving to another computer

Copy the folder. Nothing else is needed.

The browser also keeps unsaved work in its own storage and offers it back the next time the same file is opened — but only in that browser on that computer. It is a safety net, not a way to transfer work. Always save.

12.7 Version control and archiving

  • The JSON and CSV files are small text files and work well in Git (diffs show exactly what changed). Keep large scans outside Git, or use Git LFS.
  • For a publication or data repository, archive: index.html, the images, all JSON files and the CSV exports. Together they let anyone reproduce and inspect every step, including who counted what and every manual edit of the matching.

13. Why it works this way

Choice Reason
One HTML file, runs locally No installation, any operating system, works offline, data never leave the computer.
Three modules connected by files Each step can be done by a different person, checked and redone without touching the others.
Images identified by SHA-256 Everybody provably works on the same image, whatever it is called.
Paths made of segments joined into one length Step around disturbances without breaking the depth axis.
Depth = linear between two anchors per section Corrects shrinkage, keeps errors inside one section.
Sections meet exactly (end of n = start of n+1) No varve counted twice or skipped.
Blind counting, one file per counter Independent counts are what Method C needs.
No “uncertain” flag Uncertainty comes from disagreement between counters, not from self-assessment.
Tolerance relative to local varve thickness Works for thin and thick varves alike.
Strict majority; decisions cannot be overridden Objective, reproducible, as in Method C.
Separate positive and negative uncertainty Shows whether the chronology is more likely too short or too long.
Cracks only in Module 3 They do not affect counting or matching, only depths and thickness.
Horizons instead of free lines Thickness perpendicular to the lamina, also where laminae bend.
Varve numbers, no calendar ages Works for floating chronologies; anchoring is a separate, explicit step.
JSON for state, CSV for analysis Re-openable, readable, and tidy data for R.

14. Troubleshooting

Message or problem Cause and fix
“The image … is not loaded” Opening a project does not load images. Use Load images… in the Project tab.
“…content differs from the image recorded… Not loaded” The image file has changed since it was added. Use the original (12.4).
“JPEG-compressed TIFF is not supported” Re-save as uncompressed or LZW TIFF, then add it (before counting).
No DPI, or the stretch factor is far from 1 Enter the scanner's DPI or calibrate from a scale bar (5.1); check the depth anchors.
“These counts belong to P1…” Choose the right person in I am before opening a counts file.
“These counts belong to project …” The counts file was made for another project name.
“At or after the path end…” That boundary is counted at the start of the next section.
Gap or overlap between sections (Project tab) Make each section's path end equal the next section's path start (5.3).
“Load the counts of P3 first…” A chronology needs the counts of all counters it was built from.
“This chronology has no saved positions” It was saved by an older version. Open it in 2 Decide with the counts and save again.
Varve thickness says “top boundary in the previous section” First varve of a section: use a quick line (9.3).
Saving only downloads files Firefox/Safari: move the file into the project folder, or use Chrome/Edge.
Browser offers to restore unsaved changes Accept to recover work that was not saved; then save.

15. Keyboard and mouse reference

Everywhere: wheel = zoom · drag (or Space+drag, middle button) = pan · arrows = pan · F fit · R rotate view · E export image · Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo / redo · Ctrl+S save · Esc cancel.

Tab Mouse Keys
Setup click = add point · double-/right-click = finish segment · drag point = move · right-click point = delete Enter finish · Shift+click ignore joint guide · Delete remove point
1 Count click = add boundary · drag mark = move · right-click mark = delete D / A along the path · N numbers · Delete remove selected
2 Decide click mark = select group · Shift+click = merge groups X detach · C checked · . / , next / previous flag
3 Final depends on the tool (cracks on path, horizons, quick lines, cracks in varves) · right-click = finish a trace or delete Enter finish trace · [ ] previous / next boundary · K crack on line · Delete remove selected
